newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S health insurers turn to alternative medicine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S health insurers turn to alternative medicine.

text.p: When doctors diagnosed that Eric Putnoi had ulcerative colitis, they immediately prescribed drugs that he would probably have to take for the rest of his life.
But when higher doses failed to quell the pain from the bowel disorder during medical school exams, Putnoi, 28, decided he had had enough.

After a month of acupuncture and yoga, Putnoi, a first-year medical student in Boston, said he was taking less medicines and had not suffered any severe episodes, which are often triggered by stress. He attributed the change to the dual therapies, his first foray into the world of alternative medicine.

Overwhelmed by burgeoning health costs, influenced by a diverse population, and willing to try just about anything to cure ailments from AIDS to back pain, more Americans are seeking treatments not traditionally sanctioned by Western science.
Some in the health care industry are listening.
INSURERS TO FUND ALTERNATIVE MEDICINES

This month, Oxford Health Plans Incorporated will become the first major U.S. health provider to offer comprehensive coverage at pre-negotiated rates for a range of alternative health care providers, including acupuncturists, chiropractors, nutritionists, massage therapists and yoga instructors.
Unlike other health care companies, Oxford does not require a referral by the primary care physician.

"The population of this country is saying there are more professionals out there to access," said Dr Hasaan Rifaat, the Oxford executive who initiated the plan. He cited an Oxford survey that found that 33 percent of its members were already receiving some form of alternative care.
"It is an important responsibility for a health plan to ensure that we are promoting a combination of alternative and traditional care," Rifaat said.

Oxford will offer its nearly 1.5 million members a choice of packages to supplement its traditional packages. While Oxford is the only plan to offer such comprehensive coverage, several other providers now cover therapies from midwifery to massage, spurred by a groundswell of consumer demand.
"This is a member-driven world and we are responsive to what our members are asking for," said Laura Rohde, a spokeswoman with Kaiser Permanante Incorporated.
The company reimburses its seven million members for nutritional counselling, yoga classes and acupuncture. "We see it as an important trend we need to pay attention to," Rohde said.
ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE COULD ATTRACT NEW CUSTOMERS

Treatments considered "alternative" are not widely available in U.S. hospitals and are not generally taught at U.S. medical schools. The recent inclusion of these therapies in health care plans reflects both an attempt to rein in spiralling costs, and good business sense on the part of providers.

"Health plans need to market themselves in a way that differentiates them from the competition," said health care analyst John Penshorn. "If you offer a broader product line you will better satisfy existing members and be more attractive, on the balance, to new members."

Penshorn said the average employee contribution for health care premiums rose to 32 percent in 1994 from 24 percent in 1991, demonstrating that the employee is increasingly driving decisions about health care.

"Any health plan in this day and age would be foolish not to look into alternative medicine to remain competitive," said Kevin Davitt, a spokesman with Health Insurance Plan of Greater New York (HIP).
HIP began covering member visits to acupuncturists about two years ago as more Asians joined the plan, he said.

Besides appealing to current and potential members, alternative services also make sense from a broader, economic point of view. The services tend to emphasise prevention and are generally cheaper than conventional medicine, which more often requires high-tech equipment and expensive drugs, experts said.
AMERICANS SPEND MORE ON ALTERNATIVE CURES
Americans spent an estimated $13.7 billion in 1990 for alternative therapies, and the figure is growing yearly.

David Eisenberg, the director of alternative medical research at Beth Israel Hospital in Boston and Harvard Medical School, found that Americans made an estimated 425 million visits to providers of unconventional therapy during that year. In contrast, Americans made only 388 million visits to U.S. primary care providers.
Oxford's decision is also the latest step in a push toward a more holistic approach to health care. Its providers must show state licensing and demonstrate clinical experience.
